title: The Flaw of Optimism and Overpromising
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Note treats chronic overpromising as a diagnosable condition of leadership rather than a simple lapse of judgment. Its central claim is that the habit is almost never deliberate, which is why willpower is the wrong remedy: it grows out of a tangle of optimism, emotion and self-interest that each feel reasonable at the moment of commitment. The piece separates three distinct causes. Unfounded optimism leads leaders to underestimate complexity because confidence stops them short of thinking through dependencies and resource limits. Emotional discomfort leads others to say yes because declining feels like a failure of care, turning the promise into a bet on their own heroics. And strategic self-interest rewards ambitious commitments with budget and authority now while deferring the reckoning. The prescribed cure is structural rather than motivational: pressure-test commitments against real constraints before speaking, solicit dissent from people closer to the work, and keep the desire to inspire separate from the discipline to be accurate.
points: Frames overpromising as a disease with several distinct etiologies rather than a single failure of nerve or honesty.
Identifies confidence itself as the mechanism of error, since optimism stops leaders from surfacing dependencies and competing priorities before they commit.
Names the emotional variant, where saying no registers internally as a failure of care, so leaders commit to timelines they privately doubt.
Exposes the incentive logic in which ambitious promises unlock resources immediately while the cost of failure is deferred.
Argues the remedy is procedural, built on pressure-testing and invited dissent, because kept promises compound credibility in a way applause never does.
quotes: When it comes to committing to a task or assignment, leadership carries with it a peculiar temptation to say “Yes” when the more honest answer would be to decline or negotiate a more realistic expectation.
Such overpromising is rarely deliberate. It comes from a tangle of optimism, emotion, and self-interest that feels reasonable in the moment but corrodes trust over time.

For many leaders who habitually overpromise, the root cause lies in unfounded optimism. Optimistic leaders often underestimate the complexity of a task because their confidence keeps them from thinking through the constraints.
Declaring it achievable is more energizing than admitting doubt, and the commitment feels like leadership when it is actually wishful thinking dressed up like conviction.
For other leaders, emotion is the primary culprit. They find it highly discomforting to disappoint people. Saying “No” feels like a failure of care.

Committing to an ambitious outcome can unlock resources, budget, and authority in the short term. Because the reckoning for failure is deferred, the leader and the team enjoy the bounty of those resources in the present.
More importantly, they invite discussion and dissent from people closer to the work. They work hard to separate the desire to inspire from the discipline to be accurate.
The cure isn’t more willpower. It’s the discipline to let honesty outrank ambition and feel-good emotions, promise by promise.
